description: A teenage song Swift's fans refused to let her shelve: written at 16, played in tiny rooms, then rebuilt with arena guitars for Speak Now. The video is pure Speak Now World Tour — fireworks, flying balconies, costume changes and a lot of rain.

pops.text: Old song, young writer: Swift wrote 'Sparks Fly' by herself in 2006, when she was 16 — before her debut album had even come out.
She played it at small live shows in 2007, and shaky fan recordings of those performances spread online, building a cult following for a song that wasn't on any album.

The fans won. After repeated requests to release it, Swift dug the song back out, revised its lyrics several times and reworked it for her third album — the early version's banjo was removed along the way.
It's track 2 on Speak Now (2010), an album Swift wrote entirely on her own. She produced the song with her longtime early collaborator Nathan Chapman.
Speak Now debuted at No. 1 in the US with more than a million first-week sales — and every one of its 14 standard-edition songs charted on the Hot 100.
On album release in November 2010, 'Sparks Fly' debuted at No. 17 on the Billboard Hot 100 on digital sales alone — which also turned out to be its peak there.
Big Machine sent it to US country radio on July 18, 2011 as the fifth single from Speak Now — nearly five years after Swift had written it.
It climbed to No. 1 on Billboard's Hot Country Songs in November 2011, her first country chart-topper since 'You Belong with Me' in 2009, and was certified platinum in the US.

The video, directed by Christian Lamb and released August 10, 2011, is a Speak Now World Tour montage shot at four tour dates, including Newark, New Jersey — heavy on slow motion, dancers, acrobats and Swift's many costume changes. It was the tour's opening number.
Second life: 'Sparks Fly (Taylor's Version)' arrived with Speak Now (Taylor's Version) on July 7, 2023, and the re-recording reached No. 22 on the Hot 100.

title: Sparks Fly

description: A beat-driven funk-rock stomp from Phish's major-label debut, built around a tongue-twisting list of nonsense gadgets and one immortal piece of advice: whatever you do, take care of your shoes.

pops.text: Three writers share the credit: guitarist Trey Anastasio with lyricists Tom Marshall and Scott Herman — Herman was the band's less famous third pen alongside Marshall.
Big debut night: Phish first played 'Cavern' live on March 28, 1990 at Denison University in Ohio — the same show that also saw the first performances of 'Tweezer' and 'Runaway Jim.'
The studio version was recorded in the summer of 1991 at White Crow Studios in Burlington, Vermont, Phish's hometown base.
It's track 3 on A Picture of Nectar, released February 18, 1992 — the band's third album and their major-label debut for Elektra Records.
The album is a thank-you note: it's named for Nectar Rorris, owner of the Burlington bar that gave the young Phish regular early gigs and, in the band's telling, taught them how to play.
Elektra also pushed 'Cavern' as the album's second promotional single — a compact, funky calling card next to the album's longer jams.
Listen for the album title hiding in the lyric: the rapid-fire shopping list — 'a serpent deflector, a mudrat detector, a ribbon reflector' — lands on 'a cushion convector, a picture of nectar.'
The song's other immortal instruction comes early: if you've tread in primal soup, please wipe it from your shoes.
And the closing advice — 'whatever you do, take care of your shoes' — became one of the most quoted lines in the whole Phish catalogue, printed on fan shirts for decades.

Role change: in its first years 'Cavern' could turn up anywhere in a setlist, but from fall 1992 onward Phish settled it into its famous job — well over half of all performances since then have closed a set or filled the encore.

title: Cavern

description: A banjo-led barnstormer from Lifes Rich Pageant that doubles as Michael Stipe's personal credo — humor wearing thin, shirt wearing thin, and change as the one thing he believes in. This is the band's official 2024 lyric video.

pops.text: That galloping opening isn't a guitar — it's Peter Buck on banjo, an instrument the band was folding into its sound alongside piano, organ and accordion on this album.
'I Believe' sits on Lifes Rich Pageant, R.E.M.'s fourth album, released July 28, 1986 — the title deliberately drops its apostrophe.
The band recorded the album in April–May 1986 at John Mellencamp's Belmont Mall Studios in Indiana, far from their Athens, Georgia home.

Producer Don Gehman, Mellencamp's hitmaker, gave them a harder, clearer sound — and pushed Michael Stipe to enunciate, so the words land noticeably more clearly than on the band's murkier early records.
The song had an ancestor: the inner sleeve of the previous album, Fables of the Reconstruction, listed a track called 'When I Was Young,' and 'I Believe' grew up out of that earlier song.
Its belief list is pure Stipe — 'I believe in coyotes and time as an abstract' sits right next to the chorus's plainspoken punchline: 'change is what I believe in.'
It was never a single at the time — the album's only singles were 'Fall on Me' and the hidden-cover closer 'Superman' — so 'I Believe' stayed a fan-favorite album cut.
The album around it was the breakthrough step: Lifes Rich Pageant reached No. 21 on the Billboard album chart, then the band's highest placing, and became their first Gold record.
Onstage in 1989 Stipe liked to wreck his voice on this one — holding the 'I' of the final 'I believe' far past comfort until it cracked, then croaking out 'change is what I believe in.'

This video is new: R.E.M. released the official lyric video in 2024 for their voting-themed compilation We Are Hope Despite the Times. Art director Chris Bilheimer built it from Stipe's handmade T-shirt designs and the cause shirts he wore at the 1991 MTV VMAs.

title: I Believe

description: A standalone 1969 single that bridges two Stones eras — begun as a country song at Brian Jones's last session, finished with Mick Taylor's first guitar fills, and opened, famously, by a cowbell instead of a riff.

pops.text: Mick Jagger and Keith Richards wrote it on holiday in Brazil, from late December 1968 into early January 1969, after a stay on a ranch.
The band first recorded it in London in March 1969 as a country song called 'Country Honk.' Brian Jones was at those sessions — they were the last recordings he ever made with the band he founded.
Over the spring of 1969 the country tune was rebuilt into the familiar electric, riff-driven single — same song, barroom voltage turned up.
That opening beat isn't drums or guitar: it's a cowbell, played by the record's producer, Jimmy Miller.
The lead-guitar fills are a debut: 20-year-old Mick Taylor, newly hired from John Mayall's band, overdubbed them — his first appearance on a Rolling Stones recording.
The band's unofficial sixth member, Ian Stewart, plays the honky-tonk piano, with saxophones arranged by Johnny Almond rounding out the barroom sound.
The single came out in the UK on July 4, 1969 — the day after Brian Jones died. Its B-side was no throwaway either: 'You Can't Always Get What You Want.'
The next day, July 5, the Stones played it at their free Hyde Park concert — Taylor's live debut with the band, in a show that turned into a public memorial for Jones.

Chart sweep: five weeks at No. 1 in the UK — still the band's last UK No. 1 single — and four weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100 from August 23, 1969. Billboard ranked it the No. 4 song of the whole year.
Two versions live on: the original country take surfaced months later as 'Country Honk' on Let It Bleed, fiddle and all. The single itself was later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

title: Honky Tonk Women

description: A courtly tall tale — Jack the one-eyed jester, a queen, and a king waving his sword — that Panic played live for six years before recording it. This official pro-shot video is from the band's 25th anniversary run in their hometown of Athens, Georgia.

pops.text: Keyboardist John 'JoJo' Hermann had joined the band in 1992, so Ain't Life Grand — the album where 'Jack' finally landed on record — was his second studio album with Panic.
The song is far older than its album: Widespread Panic debuted 'Jack' live on August 4, 1988 at the Uptown Lounge in Athens, per Everyday Companion.
The writing credit, per the song's licensing listing, goes to John Bell, John 'JoJo' Hermann and Michael Houser — singer, keyboardist and lead guitarist.
The lyric deals a playing-card court: 'Jack was really a jester, who held his one good eye on the queen,' while the king beside her points his sword up and down with every scene.
Fans waited six years for a studio version. It finally arrived as track 10 on Ain't Life Grand, released September 6, 1994 — and it's a long one, running 7:06.
Ain't Life Grand was the band's fourth studio album, produced by Athens fixture John Keane and released on Capricorn Records; it debuted at No. 85 on the Billboard album chart.
The album closes with a secret: after 'Fishwater' comes a hidden track, Houser's solo acoustic piece 'Waiting for the Wind to Blow Down the Tree in My Backyard.'
This video is Panic on home turf: the Classic Center in Athens, February 10, 2011, opening night of the run celebrating the band's 25th anniversary. 'Jack' followed 'Pigeons' early in the second set.
Athens is where it all started — John Bell and Michael Houser met as students at the University of Georgia and began playing together around town in the early 1980s.

Houser, whose guitar voice defines the studio 'Jack,' died in 2002. By this 2011 performance the guitar chair belonged to Jimmy Herring, and 'Jack' remained a setlist regular — a song that outlived its co-writer.

title: Jack

description: Paul McCartney's dream-born hymn, filmed in the studio the day after the rooftop concert as the band was coming apart. Released as a single in March 1970, it was the Beatles' farewell record before the split went public.

pops.text: It came from a dream: during a troubled period, McCartney dreamed of his mother Mary, who had died of cancer in 1956 when he was 14. In the dream she reassured him — 'It will be all right, just let it be.'
So 'Mother Mary' is Paul's own mother, not a religious reference — though McCartney has said he doesn't mind listeners taking it that way.
He wrote and sang it, though as usual it's credited to Lennon–McCartney. He began it in late 1968, near the end of the White Album sessions.
The master take was recorded on January 31, 1969 at Apple Studios during the Get Back sessions, with Billy Preston adding organ — and John Lennon playing bass for a change.
This film was shot that same day, January 31, 1969 — the day after the famous rooftop concert — by director Michael Lindsay-Hogg. The footage has since been restored from the 16mm negative.
There are two official versions: the single, produced by George Martin, has a softer guitar solo and the orchestra mixed low.
The album version, reworked by Phil Spector, turns the orchestra and choir up and swaps in a more aggressive Harrison guitar solo — one of several Spector changes McCartney spent years objecting to.
Released as a single on March 6, 1970, it entered the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 6 — at the time the highest debut in the chart's history.
It reached No. 1 in the US for two weeks that April — knocking Simon & Garfunkel's 'Bridge Over Troubled Water' off the top — and it was the Beatles' final single before the breakup became public.

The timing was pure drama: 'Let It Be' hit No. 1 on April 11, 1970, one day after McCartney announced he was leaving the band. The Let It Be album followed in May, after the group had effectively ended.

title: Let It Be

description: The Lion King opens with no dialogue at all — just a Zulu chant over a sunrise, every animal in the Pride Lands gathering to see a newborn prince held up on Pride Rock. One of the great opening sequences in film, sung by Carmen Twillie with Lebo M.'s chant.

pops.text: That thunderous opening chant is in Zulu, sung by South African musician Lebo M. Translated, it says roughly: 'Here comes a lion, father — oh yes, it's a lion.'
Lebo M. was brought in by composer Hans Zimmer, who had scored African-set films like The Power of One. Lebo wrote and recorded the chant to match Zimmer's opening sequence.
The song itself pairs Elton John's music with Tim Rice's lyrics — the pair stepped in as Disney's songwriters for The Lion King.
The deep lead vocal in the film is Carmen Twillie's, not Elton's. Elton recorded his own pop version, backed by the London Community Gospel Choir, for the soundtrack album.

What you're watching is the film's entire opening: sunrise over the savanna, the animals journeying to Pride Rock, and Rafiki presenting baby Simba to the kingdom — finished by the title card landing on the final drumbeat.
The soundtrack album was released on May 31, 1994, a couple of weeks before the film reached cinemas.
Oscar rarity: three songs from The Lion King were nominated for Best Original Song at the same Academy Awards — this one, 'Hakuna Matata' and 'Can You Feel the Love Tonight,' which won.
'Circle of Life' was also nominated for the Grammy Award for Song of the Year, and Elton's single version charted on both sides of the Atlantic — No. 18 in the US and No. 11 in the UK.
On stage, the opening belongs to Rafiki: in the Broadway musical, which opened in 1997, the mandrill sings the chant and summons puppet animals of every size down the aisles to Pride Rock.
Twenty-five years on, Disney knew exactly what it had: the first trailer for the 2019 Lion King remake was a near shot-for-shot recreation of this opening, chant and all.

title: Circle of Life

description: Buffett's hungover Key West Sunday, from A1A: squalls on the Gulf Stream, a hammock slept in past noon, a Bloody Mary next door — and the quiet confession underneath the jokes that he can't run at this pace for long.

pops.text: Buffett wrote this one solo, and it's unusually honest for a party singer: American Songwriter reads the 'hurricane' as partly metaphor — the toll of working hard and drinking hard catching up with him.
He was only 27 when he wrote it, a year into his fame — yet the chorus already confesses, 'I could use some rest, I can't run at this pace very long.'
The opening is a Key West morning after: 'Squalls out on the Gulf Stream, big storms comin' soon — I passed out in my hammock, and God, I slept till way past noon.'

The cure he stumbles toward is next door: 'I knew I could use a Bloody Mary, so I stumbled next door to the bar' — Buffett's first Key West apartment sat beside Louie's Backyard, the local landmark of that era.
It's track 9 on A1A, running 4:21, recorded in August 1974 at Woodland Sound Studios in Nashville with producer Don Gant.

The album is named for Florida State Road A1A, the beach road running down Florida's Atlantic coast — and the song name-checks it, strolling 'down the avenue that's known as A1A' on a peculiar gray Sunday.
The song writes itself into its own last verse: the narrator walks home, sits on the beach, 'and then I made up this song.'
A1A, released in December 1974, was Buffett's fifth studio album and a breakthrough of sorts — his first to reach the upper half of the Billboard 200, peaking at No. 25.
It was never released as a single — but of all the songs on A1A, only 'A Pirate Looks at Forty' got played in concert more often than this one.
Other sailors have steered it since: Kenny Chesney and reggae singer Mishka have both covered 'Trying to Reason with Hurricane Season.'

title: Trying to Reason with Hurricane Season
Ain't Nobody
description: A live album's studio bonus track that stole the whole show — Chaka Khan rides a synth loop and a drum machine's ghost over one of the funkiest grooves of the eighties.

pops.text: Keyboardist David 'Hawk' Wolinski wrote this one for Rufus, building it around a repeating synthesizer loop — very futuristic for a funk band in 1983.
The groove started on a Linn LM-1 drum computer, but drummer John 'JR' Robinson insisted on playing real drums over it for the recording session.
Odd origin for a hit: this was one of four brand-new studio tracks tacked onto Stompin' at the Savoy, an otherwise live double album.
It was released as a single on November 4, 1983 — effectively Rufus's farewell era, with Chaka Khan already a star in her own right.
Chart report: No. 1 on Billboard's R&B chart, No. 22 on the Hot 100, and No. 8 in the UK — Rufus's final R&B chart-topper.
At the 1984 Grammy Awards it won Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal, the band's second Grammy.
Movie fans know it from the 1984 breakdancing film Breakin', whose soundtrack carried the song to a whole new audience.
The official video is a performance montage built for maximum Chaka: close-ups, big hair, bigger earrings, and that smile powering the chorus.
Though it's credited to Rufus and Chaka Khan, history files it as a Chaka Khan signature song — it's the record most people name first for her.
Decades on, the track remains a wedding, club and karaoke staple — that synth riff is instantly recognised from the first two seconds.

title: Whip It
description: Red flowerpot hats, a dude ranch, and a whip cracking clothes off a stranger — DEVO's surreal pep talk became the defining video of MTV's first year.

pops.text: Gerald Casale wrote the lyrics as an imitation of the motivational parody poems in Thomas Pynchon's novel Gravity's Rainbow — high literature, cracked like a whip.
Mark Mothersbaugh later claimed the song was a tongue-in-cheek pep talk for President Jimmy Carter ahead of the 1980 election.
Most listeners heard something far ruder in the lyrics, but the band always insisted it was a wholesome can-do anthem about solving your problems.
It's the second single from Freedom of Choice (1980), the Akron band's third album and their big move toward electronics.
Chart report: No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 — DEVO's only Top 40 hit, later certified platinum as a single.
The video's central gag came from a 1962 issue of Dude magazine: a former actor who ran a dude ranch and entertained guests by whipping his wife's clothes off daily.
Casale directed the clip himself on a set built inside the band's rehearsal space, reportedly for about $15,000 in one long day.
Those red flowerpot hats are 'energy domes,' debuted for the Freedom of Choice campaign — Casale said they were designed to channel wasted mental energy back into the brain.
MTV put the video into heavy rotation in the channel's first year, making DEVO's deadpan robots-and-cowboys look a blueprint for eighties weirdness.
Legacy check: VH1 ranked it among the greatest songs of the eighties, and everyone from Pearl Jam on down has covered it — energy domes included.

title: All I Want
description: A Santa Barbara band named for a Monty Python joke made the gentlest hit of 1992 — three minutes of jangle and yearning that still sounds like the last day of summer.

pops.text: Yes, the name is a joke: Eric Idle invented 'Toad the Wet Sprocket' for a Monty Python 'Rock Notes' sketch about a band whose lead electric-triangle player lost an elbow.
The Santa Barbara band adopted the gag name for an early gig, figured they'd change it later — then got signed before they ever did.
Singer Glen Phillips was still a teenager when the band recorded fear in Reno, Nevada — American Songwriter notes he wasn't old enough to enjoy the nightlife legally.
The band argued over the album's final track and picked 'All I Want' to complete fear, their third album, released in August 1991.
Released as a single in 1992 — slightly remixed for radio — it became the breakthrough the earlier single 'Is It for Me' hadn't managed.
Chart report: No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 4 on Top 40/Mainstream, No. 14 on Adult Contemporary and No. 10 on the Cash Box Top 100.
fear went platinum in 1994 and peaked at No. 49 on the Billboard 200 a full year after it came out — a slow-burn success story.
It wasn't a one-off: follow-up single 'Walk on the Ocean' reached No. 18, giving the band back-to-back Top 20 hits from the same album.
Story goes that Eric Idle, visiting America, was stunned to hear a DJ announce a hit by a band using the name he'd coined as a throwaway joke decades earlier.
The song later turned up in Dawson's Creek, Doogie Howser, M.D. and Homeland, and post-hardcore band Emery covered it for the 2006 compilation Punk Goes 90's.

title: Crossroads
description: Four minutes, three musicians, one borrowed blues — Cream's live Winterland detonation of Robert Johnson's standard set the bar for every guitar hero who followed.

pops.text: Robert Johnson recorded the original, 'Cross Road Blues,' in a San Antonio hotel room on November 27, 1936 — one of the most mythologised sessions in blues history.
Johnson's song feeds the famous legend of a guitarist meeting the Devil at a Mississippi crossroads to trade his soul for talent.
Cream's arrangement, devised by Eric Clapton, splices in two lines borrowed from another Johnson song, 'Traveling Riverside Blues.'
This take was recorded live at San Francisco's Winterland Ballroom on March 10, 1968, during the first of two shows that night.
Sleeve sleight of hand: the Wheels of Fire gatefold credits the live disc to the Fillmore, but 'Crossroads' is Winterland — only 'Toad' actually came from the Fillmore.
At about 4 minutes 18 seconds it's unusually compact for Cream, a band whose other live cuts on the album stretch past sixteen minutes.
Producer Felix Pappalardi captured the trio at their peak interplay: Clapton singing and soloing, Jack Bruce's bass everywhere, Ginger Baker detonating underneath.
Wheels of Fire topped the US album chart, and when 'Crossroads' was issued as a single in January 1969 it reached No. 28 on the Hot 100.
Engineer Tom Dowd later claimed the released solo was edited down from a much longer performance — a story fans and scholars still argue about, with no unedited tape ever surfacing.
Rolling Stone placed Cream's version on its 500 Greatest Songs list and near the very top of its Greatest Guitar Songs ranking; Clapton even named his 1988 box set Crossroads.

title: You'll Never Find Another Love Like Mine
description: The smoothest kiss-off ever recorded — Lou Rawls, backed by the full Philadelphia International orchestra, calmly informs an ex that the search is hopeless.

pops.text: Rawls had been a star for a decade — Grammys for 'Dead End Street' and 'A Natural Man' — but his career needed a recharge when he signed to Philadelphia International.
Label bosses Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff wrote the song for him, tailoring its smug, silky lyric to Rawls's famous four-octave baritone.
It's the lead single from All Things in Time (1976), Rawls's label debut and the only platinum album of his career.
The sound is peak Philly soul: the MFSB house band, sweeping strings and a gentle disco pulse under a ballad.
Rawls delivers the whole lyric with a smile in his voice — it's not bitter, just absolutely certain: you'll miss my lovin'.
Chart report: No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 1 on both the R&B and Easy Listening charts — the biggest hit of Rawls's life.
It was his first gold single and won an American Music Award, along with a Grammy nomination.
The follow-up, 'Groovy People,' kept the Gamble and Huff partnership charting, and Rawls won his third Grammy the next year for the album Unmistakably Lou.
Rawls parlayed the fame into good works: in 1980 he launched his Parade of Stars telethon, which raised money for the United Negro College Fund for decades.
There was no real music video era yet for Rawls — the official upload is the album audio, which is all this record needs: that voice, front and centre.

title: Our Lips Are Sealed
description: A secret romance, a convertible full of Go-Go's and a fountain finale — the opening track of Beauty and the Beat is two and a half minutes of perfect pop.

pops.text: Co-writer Jane Wiedlin had a brief romance with Terry Hall of the Specials while the Go-Go's supported them on tour in 1980 — the need for secrecy became the song.
Hall mailed Wiedlin lyrics from England; she wrote the music and added lines of her own, and the pair kept the co-writing credit — and the secret.
It's the opening track of Beauty and the Beat and was released as a single on June 12, 1981, on I.R.S. Records.
Belinda Carlisle sings most of the song, but listen for co-writer Wiedlin herself taking the bridge — 'Pay no mind to what they say...'
The album version is trimmed: the song was originally written and performed with three verses before being shortened for the record.
Chart report: No. 20 on the Billboard Hot 100, Top 5 in Australia and Canada, and No. 15 on Billboard's rock tracks chart.
Beauty and the Beat spent six weeks at No. 1 — the Go-Go's were the first all-female band who wrote their own songs and played their own instruments to top the album chart.
Derek Burbidge's video cuts a club performance with pure joyrides: the band cruising in a convertible, passing a lingerie shop, and ending up splashing in a fountain.
Hall got the last word musically: his new band Fun Boy Three recorded their own moodier version in 1983 and took it to No. 7 in the UK.
Hilary and Haylie Duff covered it for the 2004 film A Cinderella Story, introducing the Wiedlin–Hall secret to a new generation.

title: Kokomo
description: Aruba, Jamaica — and an island that doesn't exist. The Beach Boys' Cocktail comeback gave them a No. 1 a full 22 years after 'Good Vibrations.'

pops.text: The island is fictional: Kokomo is an imaginary getaway off the Florida Keys, name-checked alongside real stops like Aruba, Jamaica, Bermuda and Martinique.
The verse began as a demo by John Phillips of the Mamas & the Papas and Scott McKenzie; Mike Love and producer Terry Melcher rewrote the chorus into the travelogue everyone knows.
It was made for the Tom Cruise film Cocktail and released as a single on July 18, 1988, with Little Richard's 'Tutti Frutti' on the B-side.
Brian Wilson isn't on it — the one current member missing from the sessions. The reasons are disputed: Wilson said he was told too late; Love blamed Wilson's therapist Eugene Landy's demands.
The session band was quietly stellar: Ry Cooder on guitar and mandolin, session great Jim Keltner on drums, and Pet Sounds collaborator Van Dyke Parks on accordion.
Lead vocals trade between Mike Love and Carl Wilson, with Al Jardine and Bruce Johnston stacking those sunset harmonies behind them.
The video was shot at the brand-new Grand Floridian Resort at Walt Disney World — spot John Stamos, then a Full House star, on bongos and steel drums.
Chart report: No. 1 on the Hot 100 on November 5, 1988 — the band's first No. 1 in 22 years, a record gap between chart-toppers, and their final Top 40 hit.
It also topped the Australian chart and earned Grammy and Golden Globe nominations from its Cocktail placement.
The song was folded into the 1989 album Still Cruisin', and Wilson later joined in for a Spanish-language version — proof even Brian came around to Kokomo.
